questions.problem: Which of the following is a representation of the set $S={0,1,2}\times {-1,1}$ in the Cartesian plane?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

In this case, computing ${0,1,2}\times {-1,1}$ gives the following set:

$$
S={(0,-1),(0,1),(1,-1),(1,1),(2,-1),(2,1)}.
$$

Our visualization of this set is shown in the diagram below.

questions.problem: Which of the following is a representation of the set $S={1,2}\times (-1,1)$ in the Cartesian plane?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B={(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S={1,2}\times (-1,1)
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is either $1$ or $2$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $(-1,1).$

$$
S={(x,y)\,:\,x\in {1,2},\,y\in (-1,1)}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $(-1,1).$

$$
{S}_{1}={(1,y)\,:\,y\in (-1,1)}
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/11522acdfeaad022847fedbcf6052424216587f99f2691e80ed96152f30818a4.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $2$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $(-1,1).$

$$
{S}_{2}={(2,y)\,:\,y\in (-1,1)}.
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/90b6a9c00d366e4a03c8c974476fdf06bc9fa73c9c26e9a0cd6ba9a4bda8e66d.png)

Our Cartesian product is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
S={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is a representation of the set $S=Z\times Z$ in the Cartesian plane?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B={(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=Z\times Z
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is an integer number and whose $y$-coordinate is an integer number.

$$
S={(x,y)\,:\,x\in Z,\,y\in Z}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{-1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $-1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any integer number.

$$
{S}_{-1}={(-1,y)\,:\,y\in Z}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{-1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/9673951b4e72ba503e740369462f9e528e43ffc083706ee558ade7ccd52702f5.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{0}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $0$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any integer number.

$$
{S}_{0}={(0,y)\,:\,y\in Z}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{0}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/797b66a293eb241f841869abe97e324f4301907f71029acceefd68487bef1b4f.png)

We can create the subsets $…,{S}_{-3},{S}_{-2},{S}_{1},{S}_{2},{S}_{3},…$ similarly. Our Cartesian product $S$ is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =…\cup {S}_{-3}\cup {S}_{-2}\cup {S}_{-1}\cup {S}_{0}\cup {S}_{1}\cup \text{ }{S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}… \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in Z}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $Z\times Z$ as the set of points in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/de19fcf0f246b09d4bb957568e026b36de3f55c1a6c7065d79faacee794a8326.png)

questions.problem: Let $I=[0,1]⊂R$ and ${X}_{i}=[-i,i]\times {2i}.$ Which of the following represents ${⋃}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the union of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *at least one* set:

$$
{⋃}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for at least one}\,\,k\in I}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=0.5,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{0.5}=[-0.5,0.5]\times {1}={(k,1)\,:\,k\in [-0.5,0.5]}.
$$

This represents a horizontal line segment from the point $(-0.5,1)$ to the point $(0.5,1)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/6c6aafd9ea78868e953340eaab3862491d275972d690e2ceb27c213dadbcaea6.png)

In general,

$$
{X}_{i}=[-i,i]\times {2i}={(k,2i)\,:\,k\in [-i,i]}
$$

is the horizontal line segment from the point $(-i,2i)$ to the point $(i,2i).$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/02c8f93a25d7b510d3e238e6d4a974d6ccc2e83f3ac01fe92ce4535fbb4dce48.png)

As $i$ runs over $I,$ these line segments sweep the following triangle that represents the union ${⋃}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/3b3cefa03d71d99e4b7f3b6852ed36512d2a841a37c558034eac5c4b6870799c.png)

questions.problem: Let $I=[0,1]⊂R$ and ${X}_{i}={i}\times [0,{i}^{3}].$ Which of the following represents ${⋃}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the union of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *at least one* set:

$$
{⋃}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for at least one}\,\,k\in I}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=0.5,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{0.5}={0.5}\times [0,0.125]={(0.5,k)\,:\,k\in [0,0.125]}.
$$

This represents a vertical line segment from the point $(0.5,0)$ to the point $(0.5,0.125)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/3a1bb7a7c54718e39df80092243a119ec8b5a6e77ec4f9d58ffb074e50191d04.png)

In general,

$$
{X}_{i}={i}\times [0,{i}^{3}]={(i,k)\,:\,k\in [0,{i}^{3}]}

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Sketching Cartesian Products in the Coordinate Plane
canonical_examples.problem: Sketch a representation of the set $S = \{1, 2\} \times (0, 1)$ in the Cartesian plane.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A \times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B = \big\{(a,b) \::\: a\in A,\, b\in B\big\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S = \{1,2\} \times (0,1)
$$

contains every point in $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose $x$-coordinate is either $1$ or $2$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $(0,1).$

$$
S=
\Big\{ (x,y) \: : \: x\in \{{\color{red}{1}},{\color{blue}{2}}\},\, y\in (0,1) \Big\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider $S_1\subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals ${\color{red}{1}}$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $(0,1).$

$$
S_1 = \Big\{ ({\color{red}{1}},y) \: : \: y \in(0,1) \Big\}
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/56f200fce557749a56b9b5b51bc670da5f8c7f2cdb0196392ee80efcd6be980a.png)

Next, consider $S_2\subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals ${\color{blue}{2}}$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $(0,1).$

$$
S_2 = \big\{ ({\color{blue}{2}},y) \: : \: y \in(0,1) \big\}.
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/f96074cc265bba6eb59717364d2aa5390fdccea4d398fe5ae0b99f7ad82f0b93.png)

Our Cartesian product is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
S = S_1\cup S_2
$$

Therefore, $S$ can be represented by the two line segments shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/0c0529aaa680b4b572d17f2cfbfb76d805134e72c50ab3ed469286cc025185a3.png)

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Sketching Cartesian Products of Special Sets in the Coordinate Plane
canonical_examples.problem: Sketch a representation of the set $S = \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$ in the Cartesian plane.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A \times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B = \big\{(a,b) \::\: a\in A,\, b\in B\big\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S = \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}
$$

contains every point in $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose $x$-coordinate is an integer number and whose $y$-coordinate is a natural number.

$$
S=
\Big\{ (x,y) \: : \: x\in \mathbb Z,\, y\in \mathbb N\Big\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider $S_1\subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any integer number and whose $y$-coordinate equals ${\color{red}{1}}.$

$$
S_1 = \Big\{ (x, {\color{red}{1}}) \: : \: x\in \mathbb Z\Big\}.
$$

We can represent $S_1$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/6b63e973bbcc3e25d601a1f6cef97f5a00cc22e738c46d04a1ac06851421894e.png)

Next, consider $S_2\subset S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any integer number and whose $y$-coordinate equals ${\color{blue}{2}}.$

$$
S_2 = \Big\{ (x,{\color{blue}{2}}) \: : \: x\in \mathbb Z\Big\}.
$$

We can represent $S_2$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/f24ce8f7610d096c795a8a74b0b714b720c36442042c28b66432d6b2102fb9d4.png)

We can create the subsets $S_3,S_4,S_5,\ldots,$ similarly. Our Cartesian product $S$ is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}\cup {S}_{4}\cup … \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in N}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$ as the set of points in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/c999c61d8ffbb27d47272811e32340cef3253b4730e684be10615487a8b27200.png)

is the vertical line segment from the point $(i,0)$ to the point $(i, i^2).$
